newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader, parties agree to new government.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader, parties agree to new government.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha and leaders of all political parties signed an agreement on Sunday calling for a national unity government and elections by June in a bid to end an armed rebellion in the south.
The nine-point accord gave rebels holding several cities in the south a week to hand in weapons.

The agreement, clinched after two days of talks and mediation by senior European emissaries, followed Berisha's reversal of his earlier refusal to form a coalition with the Socialists, heirs to Albania's Communist party that ruled with an iron fist for five decades.
The June deadline for fresh elections was a further concession to the opposition, which had argued it was unrealistic to organise polls under emergency rule introduced last week.
Berisha had initially proposed new polls within 45 days and then extended this to two months.
The agreement was welcomed by the political parties, with senior Socialist official Pandeli Majko saying: "For the first time since 1990, Albanian politicians are showing maximum flexibility."

But initial reaction from rebels who have seized control of most of the south of the country appeared to be cool, and they repeated their demands for Berisha's resignation over the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes in which thousands of families lost their life savings.
The rebel leader in Gjirokaster said he was pleased with the statement and was in touch with other rebel-held towns in the south in deciding what to do.
"But at this point our position remains that Berisha must quit before we surrender our weapons," ex-general Agim Gozhita said.

Another member of the newly-elected rebel council in Gjirokaster, Murat Kaci of the Socialists, said: "Berisha has a very bad record of keeping his word and we don't believe him. We'll decide what to do when it's proven that what he says is true."

Rebels accuse the president of standing by while thousands of Albanians lost their life savings in a series of schemes that collapsed in January, sparking the initial unrest that turned into an anti-government uprising in the south.
Kaci also said the Socialists wanted the immediate release from jail of their leader Fatos Nano, jailed on corruption charges the party says were politically inspired.
Albanian state television quoted the official ATA news agency as saying initial reaction to the deal was enthusastic in Gjirokaster and the rebel stronghold of Vlore further to the south.

In Tirana, Majko of the Socialists said he was ready to go to Vlore, along with his colleagues from Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, to negotiate with the rebels as part of a national unity government.

The new arms amnesty for rebels followed a plea from the head of a European mediation mission on Saturday to prolong a 48-hour truce which ran out early on Sunday to give more time for talks and for the surrender of thousands of weapons seized by the rebels from army depots.
In Gjirokaster, which fell to the rebels on Saturday, General Gozhita took charge on Sunday, ordering teenagers to hand in their weapons and vowing to punish looters.

One person was killed and three were wounded during a night of wild celebrations after rebels seized the town, site of the main army base for the region. Army reinforcements flown in to defend it fled to the mountains.

"There will be no more shootings. Children under 18 should not carry weapons. Shops will open and those caught stealing will be punished," Gozhita told a crowd of 1,500 after he was elected president of the town's 15-member rebel council.
